claims.evidence: NHS about page summary: laxative for constipation, also used for 'a condition caused by severe liver disease called hepatic encephalopathy'. 'Causes confusion' not in NHS text seen.
claims.newSentence: Lactulose is a laxative used to treat constipation, and it is also used for hepatic encephalopathy, a condition caused by severe liver disease.

claims.evidence: About page: draws water into bowel to soften stools; at least 2 days to work. Note other NHS pages/summaries say 2 to 3 days.
NHS lactulose page: laxative to treat constipation.
Confusion/tremor/decreased consciousness wording came from UK patient leaflet (medicines.org.uk PIL 5525), not NHS. NHS says condition caused by severe liver disease.
claims.newSentence: Treating hepatic encephalopathy, a condition caused by severe liver disease.

claims.evidence: Common questions/about: osmotic laxative that draws water into bowel to soften stools.
St George's PDF appeared in results but its text was not retrieved; the sentence was not confirmed. NHS Laxatives page says osmotic laxatives draw water into bowel to soften poo.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says osmotic laxatives such as lactulose and macrogol draw water into the bowel to soften poo and make it easier to pass.

claims.evidence: 'At least 2 days' supported. '4 or 5 days' seen in one search summary of the about page, but the main NHS page and common-questions page are reported as saying 3 days; conflicting, and it is a numeric cut-off.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says lactulose is slow-acting and takes at least 2 days to work; if constipation does not improve, it advises talking to a doctor or pharmacist.

claims.evidence: Side effects page: diarrhoea very common, particularly at high doses.
Bloating and wind common, usually mild and short-lived.
Serious side effects rare; anaphylaxis possible in rare cases.
Side effects/common questions: longer use can cause prolonged diarrhoea and electrolyte imbalance.
Site signposting rule, routes to care present.
Who-can page: most adults and people 14+; under 14 needs prescription.
Retrieved: past allergic reaction to lactulose/similar medicines and galactosaemia listed; IBS also. Lactose intolerance and galactose/fructose allergies not seen.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to lactulose or a similar medicine and galactosaemia as reasons it may not be suitable.

claims.evidence: Who-can page: IBS, diverticular disease, Crohn's, bowel blockage not caused by constipation. NHS wording is tell doctor/pharmacist; some summaries say advised against.
Lactulose increases gas and bloating, which can make IBS worse.
Normal constipation amounts little/no effect; long-term high amounts may affect blood sugar. 'Many months' not seen in who-can/common-questions text (appeared in HE context).
claims.newSentence: The NHS says normal amounts of lactulose for constipation should have little or no effect on blood sugar, but long-term high amounts, such as those used for liver-related brain problems, may affect it.

claims.evidence: Pregnancy page: not harmful to baby; breastfeeding fine if doctor/midwife confirms baby healthy.
Common questions: prolonged vomiting or severe diarrhoea may stop the pill working.
Cut-off conflicts (3 days vs 4 or 5 days across NHS pages).
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises talking to a doctor or pharmacist if constipation does not improve.

claims.evidence: NHS: for HE doctor may recommend taking it for many months. Dehydration/clinician-directed claims from hospital guideline not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says that for hepatic encephalopathy a doctor may recommend taking lactulose for many months.

claims.newSentence: The NHS describes hepatic encephalopathy as a condition caused by severe liver disease, and says lactulose helps the body clear toxins that build up when the liver is failing.
